hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Sortly from a written spec. Claude passed all twenty-one checks, and found sixty-three gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Sortly a small team actually uses. Quantities for every item in every location. QR labels you scan with a phone. Low stock alerts. Purchase orders you receive against. And blind stock counts.

The core rule is movements. Stock never changes by editing a number. Every use, delivery, move and count is a movement, and the quantity on hand is their sum. Movements are never edited or deleted. And no movement can take a location below zero, so if Tom tries to use a case that isn't there, he sees: only zero on hand at Van 2.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation. Recording stock, alerts, labels and scanning. Purchase orders. Then counts and reports. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. The Items screen lists eight seed items worth one thousand one hundred and thirty-three dollars, with gloves marked low and twenty on order. The item page shows a move from the store room to a van as one row. Reorder suggestions offer twenty-four bottles of glass cleaner, but skip the gloves, because they're already on order. The label sheet prints QR codes three across. And a count review shows two differences before an admin approves them.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all twenty-one checks passed, along with one hundred and thirty-seven automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed sixty-three places where Claude had to guess. My own seed history couldn't add up to my seed table. Nothing tied a reason to a direction, so an adjustment marked Found could remove stock. And a count waiting for review didn't block a second count, so approving both would correct the same stock twice. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, the daily job on a real scheduler, or hosting. Codes were typed into the scan screen, not read by a phone camera, and the labels were never printed.

So is it worth building? Billed monthly, Sortly's Advanced plan is forty-nine dollars a month, Ultra one hundred and forty-nine, and Premium two hundred and ninety-nine, with two, five and eight user licenses. Purchase orders and stock counts start on Ultra. If one person tracks fewer than a hundred items, the free plan may be enough. If more than eight people record stock, or you want counts without paying for Ultra, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, ten rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all twenty-one checks, with the sixty-three fixes already in.
